item_title: Brent crude rose 1.5% to $97.73 a barrel, touching $97.93 — its highest since 23 July — and WTI rose 1.8% to $93.10, also a late-July high, after Saudi Aramco facilities were struck again and US and Iranian forces fired on each other's ships over the weekend.
mechanism: Saturday's CENTCOM strikes put the war on Iran's export terminal; Monday's Jizan strike puts it on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea refining outlet — and Jizan is specifically the workaround, the western routing Riyadh has leaned on to move crude without transiting Hormuz. That is the mechanism worth naming: the risk premium so far has priced a chokepoint, on the assumption that cargo which avoids the chokepoint is safe. A strike on the avoidance route prices something else, a producer-infrastructure risk that no re-routing hedges. Against capital-context.yaml's standing rate_regime read — a hawkish Fed hold into the 09-16 decision, with roughly 60% priced for a hike and the cooling-data case doing the work — a sustained oil impulse cuts directly at the disinflation premise the hold rests on. The size matters and is smaller than it first looked: Brent is +1.5% on the day and about +1.5% from Friday's corrected $96.28, not the +4.6% that a transposed baseline implied. One day is not a trend.

scenarios.direction: Brent gives back the move into Tuesday's US session as the zone proves declaratory — no boundaries published, no enforcement action — and the Jizan strike reads as a repeat of August's, which took the refinery down temporarily without changing Saudi export volumes.
scenarios.why: Rezaei announced a zone with no coordinates and a "days and weeks" timeline, and the same refinery was hit on 08-09 and in July without a durable price effect. Declaratory escalation that is not followed by capability tends to decay out of the price within days.
scenarios.precedent: The September 2019 Abqaiq/Khurais attack removed roughly 5.7 million barrels a day — far more than Jizan — and Brent's near-20% one-day spike was fully retraced within about two weeks once Aramco restored output faster than expected. Announced disruption that does not persist does not hold a premium.

scenarios.direction: Brent takes out $100 and the premium migrates from freight and war-risk insurance into the flat price, putting a headline-inflation impulse in front of the FOMC's 09-16 decision and hardening rather than deterring the hike bloc.
scenarios.why: Hegseth's sink-the-tankers statement and Ghalibaf's answer are both public commitments that are costly to walk back, and the target set has now widened from shadow-fleet vessels in transit to Iran's export terminal and Saudi refining. Goldman's own $120 risk case rests on exactly this widening.
scenarios.precedent: The 2022 energy shock is the closest modern case: an exogenous supply impulse arriving into an already-hawkish committee hardened the path rather than pausing it, because the committee read energy as feeding through to expectations. The 1973 and 1979 shocks are the older textbook versions of the same asymmetry.

context_note: Filed with a correction attached rather than as a clean read: this map carried Brent's Friday settlement as $92.68 for four days when it was $96.28, and wrote a note defending the wrong figure against correct secondary reporting. Every magnitude in this interpretation is computed off the corrected baseline. The honest caveat on the whole thing is that US cash markets were shut, so no American price has yet absorbed either the Jizan strike or the sink-the-tankers statement — Tuesday's open is the first real test of everything above.

item_title: Brent traded around $98.6 intraday, up about 1.5% from Monday's close near $97.16, and WTI reached $93.64, up 2.36% from Friday's $91.48, after Houthi strikes on Saudi Aramco facilities and four Saudi cities wounded 73 people.
mechanism: The risk premium is migrating from the chokepoint to the workaround. Hormuz's closure pushed Saudi crude onto the Red Sea route, and the Red Sea route is now what gets hit. That changes what the premium is pricing: not the probability that one strait closes, but the absence of any routing that is out of range. A premium on a chokepoint is arbitrageable by re-routing; a premium on the re-routing itself is not, which is why the same headline dollar move is a worse fact this week than it was in July.

scenarios.direction: Brent holds a floor well above the pre-war band even on de-escalation headlines
scenarios.why: With both the primary route and its substitute demonstrated to be in range, buyers have to price physical delivery risk rather than transit risk, and that does not unwind on a diplomatic headline the way a chokepoint premium does.
scenarios.precedent: The September 2019 Abqaiq/Khurais strikes removed 5.7 million barrels a day — about half of Saudi output — and Brent's initial spike faded within weeks once spare capacity and reserves were confirmed. The distinguishing feature then was that the alternative routes were untouched; that is the condition now absent.

scenarios.direction: OPEC+ spare capacity caps the move short of a sustained triple-digit break
scenarios.why: The group left October output flat into a rising price, which is the behaviour of a producer bloc that believes it retains the option to add barrels later and prefers to bank the price now. If that read is right, the ceiling is policy, not geology.
scenarios.precedent: Through the 2022 Russian-invasion spike, OPEC+ repeatedly declined to accelerate quota increases while prices ran, then normalised output as the premium decayed — the same hold-then-normalise pattern.

context_note: conflict_risk_premium in the standing snapshot already records the Iran war as widening rather than resolving on every front, with the Iran-Oman reopening deal stuck at "final drafts." Today extends that reading rather than changing it; what is new is the target class, not the direction.

item_title: The yen hit a seven-month high on Bank of Japan hike expectations, taking the Nikkei down 1,130 points.
mechanism: A carry unwind and an oil shock arrived in the same session and are being read as one risk-off tone, but they transmit through different channels and the tell is in the cross-rates: the yen moved 1.45% while the dollar index moved 0.31%. That gap says the move is funding-currency repricing on BOJ hike expectations, not a flight into dollars. Carry unwinds hit levered positions in whatever they funded, which in 2026 disproportionately means the AI-buildout trade.

scenarios.direction: A sustained BOJ tightening path pressures AI-complex equities more than the oil move does
scenarios.why: Yen-funded leverage is a real component of the positioning behind the capex trade, and a rising funding cost forces deleveraging regardless of what the underlying fundamentals do. The Dow's −1.17% against the S&P's −0.48% today is the wrong shape for an oil-led selloff and the right shape for a positioning one.
scenarios.precedent: The 5 August 2024 unwind, after the BOJ's late-July hike, took the Nikkei down 12.4% in a session and dragged global tech with it on no change in tech fundamentals — the cleanest recent case of a funding-currency move repricing an unrelated equity complex.

scenarios.direction: The move stalls as a repricing of one BOJ meeting and does not become a funding shock
scenarios.why: A seven-month high is a round-trip to levels seen this year, not a regime break, and the Nikkei's 1.7% is an order of magnitude short of a genuine unwind.
scenarios.precedent: Multiple 2025 yen rallies on hike speculation reversed within weeks when the BOJ held, with no lasting cross-asset transmission.

context_note: cross_border_credit records global cross-border bank claims at $47.62T and rising — the balance-sheet channel a funding shock would travel through. That reading is the reason to treat a yen move as more than a Japan story.

item_title: The White House's pressure on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh intensified into a meeting where the market's own question has flipped from whether the Fed cuts to whether it hikes.
mechanism: The political economy of Fed independence usually gets tested when a president wants easier policy and the data are ambiguous. This is the harder version: an oil-driven inflation impulse gives the hawks a concrete case at the exact moment the political pressure is for cuts, so any decision is legible as a political one. The independence cost is asymmetric — cutting reads as capitulation whatever the data say, while hiking reads as defiance, and only one of those is recoverable.

scenarios.direction: The Fed holds again and the dissent count grows rather than the rate changing
scenarios.why: A hold is the only outcome that is not immediately legible as a response to the White House, and the August meeting already carried three dissents for a hike — the committee has a way to express hawkishness without the chair having to own a move.

scenarios.direction: The long end, not the front end, does the tightening
scenarios.why: If markets doubt the Fed can hike into political pressure, the term premium carries the inflation risk instead. The 30-year at 5.231% is where that would show up first, and it has risen 6bp over two weeks while the 10-year sat still.

context_note: rate_regime records a hawkish hold at 3.50–3.75% with three dissents for a hike, up from unanimous in June, and the 09-07 interpretation carried roughly 60% priced for a hike into the 09-16 decision. ⚠️ Marked speculative deliberately: that figure is days old, and today's "markets now expect a hike" claim comes from press reporting — neither has been checked against a live futures curve.
